record_type_quote: This research replicates an earlier study (O’Connor, Beach, Sanchez, Bocian, & Flynn, 2015) and extends it by shifting instructional responsibility from researchers to special education teachers, who implemented reading instruction that included multisyllabic word decoding, academic vocabulary, and three comprehension strategies (generating main ideas, comparing and contrasting people, and events, and identifying cause and effect relations) with their intact 8th grade history classes, using history text as the reading material.

targets.authors: O’Connor, R.E., Beach, K., Sanchez, V. Bocian, K., and Flynn, L.
targets.title: Building BRIDGES: A Design Experiment to Improve Reading and United States History Knowledge of Poor Readers in 8th Grade.
targets.evidence_quote: This research replicates an earlier study (O’Connor, Beach, Sanchez, Bocian, & Flynn, 2015) and extends it by shifting instructional responsibility from researchers to special education teachers, who implemented reading instruction that included multisyllabic word decoding, academic vocabulary, and three comprehension strategies (generating main ideas, comparing and contrasting people, and events, and identifying cause and effect relations) with their intact 8th grade history classes, using history text as the reading material.
targets.outcome_quote: We expected improvement in decoding and vocabulary because gains had been strong in the previous two years when researchers implemented the lessons in small groups. These processes (often referred to as “bottom-up”) are necessary when they constrain students’ ability to apply taught strategies to derive meaning from text (Kintsch, 2005). Nonetheless, in the current study teachers implemented lessons and their instructional groups were larger than in the earlier years of researcher-delivered lessons, so we did not expect to see gains as large as we found here, especially since other research that has shifted instruction from researchers to teachers has shown drops in student gains when teachers implement practices with their intact classes (e.g., Berkeley et al., 2010).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original gains are explicitly stated; current gains in decoding and vocabulary were unexpectedly large even under teacher implementation. The conclusion reports strong reading and history gains. General limitations do not state that this attempt cannot adjudicate the effect.

reasoning: New schools and classrooms re-test the published BRIDGES finding; one original paper is explicitly named.
